The *Rājadharmakāṇḍa* is one of the sections (*kāṇḍas*) of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Lakṣmīdhara Bhaṭṭa, the foreign minister of King Govindacandra of Kānyakubja (r. 1100–1160 A.D.). None of...
Only the following *kāṇḍas* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru* have been published to date.
According to a manuscript described by Professor Peterson in *Report No. 1* (1882–3, p.
108), the complete work *Kṛtyakalpataru* consists of the following:
In the *Kāṇḍas*:
(1) *Brahmacārikāṇḍa*, concerning the unmarried Vedic student, [the first].
(2) Gṛhasthakāṇḍa, concerning the duties, fasts, and festivals of the householder; (Second).
(3) Naiyatakālakāṇḍa, concerning the daily duties of the householder.
Holder, (Third).
(4) Śrāddhakāṇḍa, concerning funeral ceremonies, (Fourth). (5) Dānakāṇḍa, concerning religious gifts, (Fifth).
(6) *Pratiṣṭhākāṇḍa*, concerning the consecration of images; (Sixth) (7) *Tīrthakāṇḍa*, concerning pilgrimage to sacred sites;
(Eighth).
(8) *Śuddhikāṇḍa*, on purification, (the tenth);
(9) *Rājadharmakāṇḍa*, on the duties of kings, (the eleventh);
(10) *Vyavahārakāṇḍa*, on legal procedure, (the twelfth).
(11) *Śāntikāṇḍa*, on propitiatory rites, (the thirteenth).
(12) *Mokṣakāṇḍa*, on liberation, (the fourteenth).

This concerns the arrangement of the contents of the *Rājadharma-kāṇḍa*.
The *Rājadharma-kāṇḍa* is in the form of a digest of Hindu political thought. It consists primarily of extracts from ancient authorities on the subject at hand. — Lakṣmīdhara.
He takes up a subject and, regarding that subject, cites a number of authoritative sources;
very rarely does he offer his own notes or comments in connection with the texts he has quoted.
His citations are not strictly in chronological order. Let us examine Chapter V, which discusses fortifications. His first author—
The Ṛgveda is Yājñavalkya; then comes Manu, then the Matsyapurāṇa,
then Manu again, Bṛhaspati, then Manu for a third time, Bṛhaspati again,
the Matsyapurāṇa for a third time, and Bṛhaspati for a third time— the Matsya...
The *Devīpurāṇa* is the third among the Purāṇas.
The twenty-two chapters of the *Rājadharmakāṇḍa* can be divided into seven well-defined units of political thought.
(1) Lakṣmīdhara dedicates the first ten chapters to the exposition of the seven constituent elements (*prakṛti*) that comprise the state.
For instance, the first three chapters treat of the first element, namely:
The fourth chapter deals with the second element, namely the ministers, following the discussion of the king’s appreciation, consecration, and qualifications.
In the fifth chapter, the third element, the fortress, is discussed.
The sixth and seventh chapters concern territory.
Element. The fifth, sixth, and seventh elements—namely, the treasury, the army, and the ally—are discussed respectively in the eighth, ninth, and tenth chapters. The eleventh chapter deals with...

Far-sighted (*dīrghadarśī*) means one who knows the true nature of future tasks. Profound (*gambhīra*) means one whose outward expressions of anger, joy, and so forth are unobservable. One whose secret counsel is hidden (*gūḍhamantrapracāraḥ*) means one whose true nature of counsel is inferred only from its results. S 7 . - The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. “Monks, physical food, whether coarse or subtle, is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Contact is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Mental volition is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Consciousness is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. “Monks, if there were no physical food, whether coarse or subtle, would the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and the support of those seeking a new existence, be possible? “No, indeed, Blessed One. “Therefore, monks, it is to be understood: ‘Physical food, whether coarse or subtle, is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. “Monks, if there were no contact, would the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and the support of those seeking a new existence, be possible? “No, indeed, Blessed One. “Therefore, monks, it is to be understood: ‘Contact is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. “Monks, if there were no mental volition, would the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and the support of those seeking a new existence, be possible? “No, indeed, Blessed One. “Therefore, monks, it is to be understood: ‘Mental volition is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. “Monks, if there were no consciousness, would the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and the support of those seeking a new existence, be possible? “No, indeed, Blessed One. “Therefore, monks, it is to be understood: ‘Consciousness is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. “Monks, when one sees thus with right wisdom as it really is, the craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there, is abandoned; by its abandonment, future birth is abandoned; by the abandonment of birth, aging and death are abandoned; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are abandoned. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, the Blessed One has taught us these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Friends, physical food, whether coarse or subtle, is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Contact is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Mental volition is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Consciousness is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Then the Venerable Udāyin approached the Venerable Ānanda and said: “Friend Ānanda, what is the nutriment for consciousness? “Friend, the nutriment for consciousness is contact. “But friend, what is the nutriment for contact? “Friend, the nutriment for contact is feeling. “But friend, what is the nutriment for feeling? “Friend, the nutriment for feeling is contact. “Friend, you have turned back upon yourself, friend; you have returned to the very point from which you set out. “Friend, how is it that you say: ‘Friend, the nutriment for consciousness is contact’; and then: ‘But friend, what is the nutriment for contact?’—‘Friend, the nutriment for contact is feeling’; and then: ‘But friend, what is the nutriment for feeling?’—‘Friend, the nutriment for feeling is contact’? “Friend, it is just as if a man were to drive a wedge between two planks that are joined together. Even so, friend, when consciousness is conditioned by contact, and contact is conditioned by consciousness, it is through this conditionality and causal dependence that there is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.

Thus spoke the Venerable Udāyin. Having said this, he rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred, exactly as it had been said. O Śakra! [This was done] by Vasu, by the high-souled Dakṣa who desires offspring, by me, by Viṣṇu, and by Rudra together with Umā.
And having perceived himself cast down into the stream in his true form,
the Goddess, the bestower of all desires, appeared in his presence.
Therefore, O Indra among kings! you too should cause the Vasordhārā to be bestowed;
there is no merit greater than this, O best of monarchs! (85)
Even for a single day, the performance of the Vasordhārā offering should be undertaken by a king who desires prosperity and wishes to conquer the kingdoms of others. (86)
O child! Know that this continuous stream [of oblations] must always be offered for the destruction of enemies;
the interruption of the daily homa must never be allowed under any circumstances. (87)
He who causes the gods to turn away incurs a great fault.
O King, in the absence of materials, in the absence of ghee, or when there is fear arising from thieves,
if the stream does not flow, then no defect exists.

O best of kings! Having performed the fire-sacrifice (homa), one should ask forgiveness from the god and the goddess; O dear one, when [the image] is brought back again, the installation should be performed according to the prescribed injunctions. || 86 ||
In the great month of Āśvina, on the eighth and ninth lunar days, as well as on the full moon of Kārtika, Māgha, and Caitra, and under the asterisms of Citrā and Rohiṇī; || 60 ||
O best of beings, Jyeṣṭhā should be offered on the full moon of Vaiśākha;
the twelfth day of Āṣāḍha is prescribed, as well as the eighth and the full moon of Nabhas.
O child! On the fourth lunar day of the month of Nabhasya, under the Rohiṇī asterism and on a Tuesday, as well as during all solar transits (saṅkrāntis) occurring on Thursday or Saturday; || 12 ||
It should be bestowed during lunar and solar eclipses, at the rite of consecration, during sacrificial ceremonies,
on the festival of a son's birth, and during the ritual bathing with flowers.
On the path, when there is a binding of vows that is most terrible, and when a comet is seen—1.

(136) For the pacification of household duties, the auspicious stream should be bestowed.
Thus, one who causes the stream to flow according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures—
For him, the entire earth, together with its mountains and oceans, is successfully accomplished.
Merit equal to that of an Aśvamedha sacrifice arises from a daily fire-oblation, as does the merit of a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices.
For one who performs a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices at night, mental anxieties and physical ailments never arise at any time.
One shall obtain long life, health, and sovereignty, and at its conclusion, one shall become happy. || 67 ||

Thus ends the section on the Duties of Kings (*rājadharma-kāṇḍa*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara Bhaṭṭa, the minister for peace and war (*sāndhivigrahika*) to the great king Śrīmad Govindacandra.
